abstract: In this white paper, we highlight the importance of the ($1-10~{\rm Hz}$) frequency range for laboratory tests of the quantum nature of gravity using the quantum gravity-induced entanglement of masses (QGEM) protocol. QGEM requires matter-wave interferometers with masses ($m\sim10^{-15}-10^{-14}~{\rm kg}$), brought within separations ($d\sim30-50~μ{\rm m}$), while maintaining spatial superpositions of ($1-20~μ{\rm m}$) and coherence for ($τ\sim 0.1 - 1~{\rm s}$). These requirements make low-frequency environmental noise a central experimental challenge and place QGEM in a regime closely related to the low-frequency goals of the Einstein Telescope (ET) and the Cosmic Explorer (CE). In particular, QGEM is sensitive to relative acceleration noise (RAN) and to gravity-gradient noise (GGN) generated by seismic and other environmental mass-density fluctuations. For representative parameters $m=10^{-14}~{\rm kg}$, $Δx=10~μ{\rm m}$, and $τ=1~{\rm s}$, the differential acceleration-noise amplitude spectral density must be suppressed well below the $10^{-15}~{\rm m\,s^{-2}/\sqrt{Hz}}$ level to keep acceleration-induced dephasing below the relevant experimental scale. Achieving this level of low-frequency noise suppression is therefore a key requirement for QGEM and closely parallels the seismic and gravity-gradient noise challenges that ET and CE address.
summary: This white paper outlines a method to test quantum gravity by measuring the entanglement of masses using a matter-wave interferometer operating in the $1-10 	ext{ Hz}$ range. The core challenge is suppressing environmental noise, requiring unprecedented stability comparable to next-generation gravitational-wave detectors. It provides a theoretical roadmap for realizing quantum gravity tests using advanced atom interferometry.
main_problem: The paper addresses the feasibility of using matter-wave interferometers to test the quantum nature of gravity by measuring the spin entanglement witness for quantum gravity effects.
main_result: The required sensitivity to environmental noise, particularly relative acceleration noise, must be below $10^{-15} 	ext{ m s}^{-2}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$ in the $1-10 	ext{ Hz}$ band, placing the experiment in a regime comparable to advanced gravitational-wave detectors.
method: The analysis involves theoretical modeling of the Quantum Gravity-Induced Entanglement of Masses (QGEM) protocol using matter-wave interferometry.
model_or_system: The system is a matter-wave interferometer designed to maintain spatial superpositions ($\Delta x \sim 1-20 \mu	ext{m}$) and coherence ($	au \sim 0.1-1 	ext{ s}$) using masses ($m \sim 10^{-15}-10^{-14} 	ext{ kg}$).
key_observables: The spin entanglement witness, phase difference ($\Delta\phi$), and sensitivity to Relative Acceleration Noise (RAN) and Gravity-Gradient Noise (GGN).
important_parameters: Frequency range of $1-10 	ext{ Hz}$; required noise suppression below $10^{-15} 	ext{ m s}^{-2}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$; mass $m=10^{-14} 	ext{ kg}$.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes standard quantum mechanics and general relativity, and the primary limitation is environmental noise suppression.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QGEM protocol, details the experimental requirements for the interferometer (mass, separation, coherence), analyzes the dominant low-frequency noise sources (RAN, GGN), and compares the necessary noise suppression levels to those targeted by large-scale gravitational-wave observatories like ET and CE.
why_interesting: This work bridges fundamental quantum gravity tests with cutting-edge experimental challenges in low-frequency sensing, directly connecting quantum information concepts (entanglement witnesses) to macroscopic physics and detector technology.
